paragraphs: This paper studies sequences whose measurements live in a curved mathematical space rather than an ordinary space of numerical vectors. Its focus is symmetric positive definite matrices. When such measurements arrive over time, a model needs to capture both their sequential relationships and the geometry of the space they inhabit.

The authors develop a statistical recurrent network for this setting. Recurrence provides a way to connect successive observations, while the manifold formulation accommodates their non-Euclidean structure. The contribution includes an efficient algorithm and a rigorous study of its statistical properties, connecting the proposed network architecture with an analysis of how it behaves.

Numerical experiments show performance competitive with leading methods while using substantially fewer parameters. That finding suggests the geometric structure can support a compact model without giving up competitive results in the evaluated settings. The paper also applies the approach to statistical analysis in brain imaging, illustrating its relevance to a domain where these structured measurements arise.
neurips-2018-a-statistical-recurrent-mod.tldr: A recurrent statistical model handles manifold-valued sequences and achieves competitive experimental results with substantially fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation asks how knowledge learned in one setting can remain useful in another. This paper addresses the case where several source domains contribute information to an unsupervised target-domain adaptation problem. Multiple sources introduce multiple shifts in the data, so a representation must account for more than a single source-to-target mismatch.

The authors derive generalization bounds for both classification and regression. These bounds motivate multisource domain adversarial networks, or MDAN. The networks learn features that resist differences among domains while retaining information needed for the prediction task. Their training objective is tied to task-adaptive generalization bounds, giving the adversarial learning strategy a theoretical basis.

Experiments cover sentiment analysis, digit classification, and vehicle counting, with reported superior adaptation performance across classification and regression tasks. These results support the usefulness of treating multiple domain shifts together. The central contribution is the connection between a theoretical account of transfer and a practical neural-network method for learning representations that remain predictive across those shifts.
neurips-2018-adversarial-multiple-source.tldr: MDAN uses generalization bounds to guide adversarial learning from multiple source domains for classification and regression.

paragraphs: Missing readings create two connected problems for time-series analysis: reconstructing the absent values and making predictions from the completed sequence. When several signals are correlated, their missing entries may also need to be estimated together. BRITS addresses this setting with a recurrent neural network that learns how to fill the gaps.

Its key design choice is to make the missing values variables inside a bidirectional recurrent computation. Training can then update these values through backpropagation along with the network. Processing the sequence in both directions connects an estimate to temporal information on either side. The method does not require a specified data-generating model such as linear state-space dynamics.

The approach can handle correlated missing values and nonlinear underlying dynamics. Evaluations use air-quality measurements, healthcare data, and localization data for human activity. BRITS outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods on both reconstruction accuracy and classification or regression accuracy. The findings connect better treatment of missing observations with improved performance on the tasks that use those observations.
neurips-2018-brits-bidirectional-recurre.tldr: BRITS learns missing time-series values inside a bidirectional recurrent network, improving imputation and downstream prediction in its evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper tackles causal discovery from observational data: using recorded variables to infer causal structure without intervening on the system. Its proposed method, Kernel Conditional Deviance for Causal Inference, or KCDC, builds on the idea that the relationship from cause to effect can have a different statistical character from the reverse relationship.

The authors introduce an interpretation of this directional asymmetry and turn it into a mathematical measure using reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. The approach is fully nonparametric, avoiding a prescribed finite-dimensional family for the relationships being examined. From the asymmetry measure, they develop three decision rules that translate the statistical comparison into causal-discovery decisions.

Tests on varied synthetic datasets provide evidence of broad applicability and robustness within those evaluations. The paper also evaluates real-world time series and the Tübingen Cause-Effect Pairs benchmark, reporting performance beyond state-of-the-art approaches. These findings support the proposed asymmetry measure as a useful signal for causal discovery, rather than establishing that observational data always determine causal direction.
neurips-2018-causal-inference-via-kernel.tldr: KCDC uses a nonparametric kernel measure of cause-effect asymmetry to infer causal structure from observational data.

paragraphs: Kleinberg's impossibility result shows that three proposed requirements for clustering cannot all hold simultaneously. One requirement, consistency, says a clustering should stay unchanged when members of each group become more similar and different groups become less similar. This paper examines why that seemingly helpful modification can still create a conflict.

The authors identify changes in the appropriate number of clusters as a source of the problem. They use cost functions to determine that number and revise consistency so it applies only when the number remains unchanged. This makes the requirement conditional on the grouping scale staying stable, rather than demanding the same partition across every qualifying modification.

They prove that single linkage satisfies the revised axioms. For inputs that are well-clusterable, some other popular procedures, including k-means, also satisfy them. The distinction matters: the k-means result depends on the structure of the input. The work offers a compatible set of requirements and helps explain why familiar clustering objectives can guide successful algorithms.
neurips-2018-clustering-redemptionbeyond.tldr: Conditioning clustering consistency on an unchanged cluster count yields compatible axioms satisfied by single linkage and, on well-clusterable inputs, k-means.

paragraphs: Physical systems evolve continuously, while many reinforcement-learning methods organize decisions into discrete time steps. Turning continuous dynamics into such steps can introduce approximation error. This paper addresses value-function approximation directly in continuous time, aiming to provide more flexibility than the limited existing techniques available for that setting.

The authors propose a model-based framework in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. These spaces provide the mathematical setting for kernel-based function approximation. The framework accommodates approaches including Gaussian processes and kernel adaptive filters, allowing different kernel methods to be used within a shared treatment of continuous-time value estimation rather than prescribing one fixed approximation technique.

The stated flexibility includes handling uncertainty and nonstationarity without prior knowledge about the environment or a predetermined choice of basis functions. Experiments demonstrate the validity of the framework. Its contribution is therefore a general foundation for continuous-time approximation: it connects direct treatment of system dynamics with kernel methods that can adapt how a value function is represented.
neurips-2018-continuous-time-value-funct.tldr: A kernel-based framework provides flexible model-based value-function approximation directly in continuous time.

paragraphs: The output activation is the part of a neural network that turns its learned internal representation into a final prediction. This paper changes that component by replacing the commonly used softmax function with a new interpolating function. The proposed change therefore concerns how learned features produce outputs, while remaining part of a deep-network architecture.

The authors provide training and testing algorithms for the resulting model, including end-to-end training. They describe the framework as combining advantages of deep learning and manifold learning. The motivation is to bring those two approaches together at the prediction stage, using an interpolating output function within a trainable neural system.

Compared with conventional networks using softmax, the paper reports better applicability when training data are insufficient and significant generalization improvements across a wide variety of networks. These findings suggest that output-layer design can materially affect learning from limited examples and prediction on unseen data. A PyTorch implementation accompanies the approach, making the proposed architecture and algorithms available as an implemented method.
neurips-2018-deep-neural-nets-with-inter.tldr: Replacing softmax with an interpolating output function improves reported generalization and suitability for limited training data.

paragraphs: Many interactions happen at irregular, uncertain times instead of at evenly spaced steps. This paper studies how an agent can choose interventions when both its actions and the feedback it receives take the form of discrete events in continuous time. Marked temporal point processes describe both the timing of events and their associated types or attributes.

The agent's policy is defined through its event intensity and mark distribution, connecting decisions about when to act with decisions about what action to take. The authors derive a policy-gradient method and use deep recurrent networks to encode the action and feedback histories as numerical vectors. The method does not prescribe a functional form for the feedback intensity or mark distribution.

The framework also allows arbitrarily complex reward functions. Applications to viral marketing and personalized teaching use data from Twitter and Duolingo. The reported evidence suggests that the method may find interventions that help marketers and learners more effectively than alternatives. That qualified finding supports its potential in asynchronous interaction settings without asserting universal intervention effectiveness.
neurips-2018-deep-reinforcement-learning.tldr: A policy-gradient method learns when and how to intervene in continuous-time systems with irregular action and feedback events.

paragraphs: Collaborative learning lets multiple data owners build a model from their combined information while keeping their datasets private. This paper combines secure multi-party computation with differential privacy. Secure computation supports combining information without exposing the underlying private inputs, while differential privacy adds noise to the results that are released.

The authors develop two approaches. In output perturbation, the participants combine locally trained models inside a secure computation and add noise before releasing the combined model. In gradient perturbation, they jointly train a global model over multiple iterations, securely aggregate local gradients, and add noise before revealing each update.

The central result is that adding noise after aggregation, while still inside the secure computation, can reduce the noise required in the multi-party setting. Both approaches asymptotically improve on the best previous results described by the paper. Experiments on real-world datasets show substantial gains in model utility for typical privacy requirements, linking the improved noise treatment to more useful collaborative learning.
neurips-2018-distributed-learning-withou.tldr: Securely aggregating models or gradients before adding differential-privacy noise improves the utility of distributed learning.

paragraphs: Isotonic regression fits values while requiring them to respect an ordering. This paper studies optimization with such ordering constraints when the objective is submodular and potentially non-convex. The challenge is to retain the useful flexibility of non-convex objectives while finding a formulation that supports efficient computation.

The authors show that the problem can be expressed as a convex optimization problem over one-dimensional measures. In that representation, the ordering constraints become first-order stochastic-dominance constraints. The important change is the space in which optimization happens: a problem that may be non-convex in its original form receives a convex formulation in the new space.

New discretization schemes turn this formulation into algorithms using function values, first-order information, or higher-order information. The algorithms also improve optimization without isotonic constraints. In experiments, non-convex loss functions can be much more resistant to outliers in isotonic regression, while the considered problems remain solvable in polynomial time. The result connects computational tractability with an empirically useful choice of loss.
neurips-2018-efficient-algorithms-for-no.tldr: A convex reformulation enables efficient submodular optimization with ordering constraints and supports outlier-robust non-convex isotonic regression.

paragraphs: An error bound condition describes how an objective grows as a candidate solution moves away from the set of optimal solutions. Such conditions can help explain fast optimization. This paper examines their consequences for statistical learning, where the goal is to control prediction risk using a finite collection of samples.

The authors establish rates for empirical risk minimization under error bound conditions in settings involving Lipschitz continuity and smooth convex random functions. They also analyze an efficient stochastic-approximation algorithm for Lipschitz continuous random functions. That algorithm processes the samples in a single pass, connecting the statistical guarantees with a computationally economical learning procedure.

Depending on the power constant in the error bound condition, the rates range from approximately 1/√n to 1/n, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Empirical risk minimization can be faster than 1/n in special cases. Crucially, both approaches adapt to the condition without being given knowledge of it. The results explain how favorable objective structure can improve learning rates automatically.
neurips-2018-fast-rates-of-erm-and-stoch.tldr: Error bound conditions yield automatically adaptive learning rates for empirical risk minimization and a one-pass stochastic algorithm.

paragraphs: Recognizing each image region independently can overlook relationships among the objects in a scene. This becomes especially problematic when rare categories have few examples and many categories are easy to confuse. The paper introduces Hybrid Knowledge Routed Modules, or HKRM, to bring semantic relationships into large-scale object detection.

The method uses two forms of knowledge. An explicit module represents structured information expressed through language, such as shared attributes and relationships between concepts. An implicit module captures constraints such as common spatial arrangements. Both operate on a graph connecting image regions, adapting their reasoning to the visual evidence in each image.

The modules are described as lightweight, general-purpose additions that can incorporate multiple kinds of knowledge into detection networks. Experiments report roughly 34.5% improvement in mAP on VisualGenome with 1,000 categories and 30.4% on ADE. These results support using scene-level semantic reasoning to improve region-level recognition, particularly in the challenging large-category setting that motivates the work.
neurips-2018-hybrid-knowledge-routed-mod.tldr: HKRM combines explicit semantic knowledge and implicit scene constraints to improve large-scale object detection.

paragraphs: Image inpainting fills a missing region using the surrounding image as context. A successful completion needs both coherent overall structure and convincing small details. This paper proposes a generative multi-column convolutional network that synthesizes different image components in parallel within a single stage, addressing these requirements through a coordinated architecture.

The training objective gives global structure and local detail distinct roles. A confidence-driven reconstruction loss helps characterize the image's overall organization. An implicit diversified Markov random field regularizer encourages richer local detail. Together with the network, these losses propagate information from the visible context into the region being reconstructed.

The authors evaluate the method on challenging street views, faces, natural objects, and scenes. They report visually compelling completions even without post-processing that had commonly been used previously. The finding supports the combination of parallel synthesis and complementary training objectives: the network can bring local and global contextual information together within the inpainting process itself.
neurips-2018-image-inpainting-via-genera.tldr: A parallel multi-column network combines global reconstruction and local-detail objectives to produce compelling image completions without common post-processing.

paragraphs: Online algorithms must make decisions while information is still arriving. Machine-learned predictions offer a way to inform those decisions, but their usefulness depends on how accurate they are. This paper studies how an online algorithm can benefit from predictions while remaining resilient when the predictor provides poor guidance.

The authors develop new algorithms for two classical problems: ski rental and non-clairvoyant job scheduling. In both settings, predictions influence the choices the algorithm makes. A central property is that the algorithms do not need to know the predictor's performance in advance. Their operation therefore does not require a supplied assessment of prediction quality.

The stated results combine two desirable behaviors: performance improves as predictions improve, and poor predictions cause only limited degradation. The contribution is a way to connect predictive learning with online decision-making while accounting for unreliable forecasts. Its significance lies in that combination: the algorithms can use better information when it is available without requiring the predictor to be consistently accurate.
neurips-2018-improving-online-algorithms.tldr: Prediction-assisted algorithms for ski rental and job scheduling improve with better forecasts while limiting degradation from poor ones.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders learn hidden representations that can support data generation, but those representations are often difficult to understand or control. This paper focuses on organizing features correlated with binary labels into interpretable parts of the hidden representation. The aim is to make particular attributes easier to inspect and manipulate.

The proposed Conditional Subspace VAE, or CSVAE, learns a low-dimensional latent subspace associated with each label. Mutual-information minimization is part of the mechanism used to organize these subspaces. Instead of leaving all learned variation in an undifferentiated representation, the model gives label-associated features an explicit place within its latent structure.

The authors demonstrate attribute manipulation on the Toronto Face and CelebA datasets. These demonstrations show the utility of representations whose label-associated subspaces can be inspected and independently manipulated. The claim concerns features correlated with the labels: the paper's contribution is a controllable organization of learned variation, with practical examples of using that organization to alter attributes in generated data.
neurips-2018-learning-latent-subspaces-i.tldr: CSVAE organizes features correlated with binary labels into interpretable latent subspaces that support independent attribute manipulation.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how an agent can develop useful behavior through curiosity when its environment provides no clear external reward. In a simulated setting, the agent can move and interact with visible objects. The learning system separates predicting the world from estimating where those predictions are likely to fail.

A world-model network learns the consequences of the agent's actions. Alongside it, an explicit self-model learns the pattern of errors made by the world model. The agent uses this second model to challenge its developing predictor, directing exploration toward novel and informative interactions. Here, self-awareness refers to tracking predictive errors through a separate learned model.

The resulting behavior includes ego-motion prediction, object attention, and object gathering. The learned world model also supports improved object-dynamics prediction, detection, localization, and recognition. These results connect curiosity-driven interaction with useful visual and physical representations. The authors present the work as an initial step toward flexible agents that can supervise their own learning in realistic physical environments.
neurips-2018-learning-to-play-with-intri.tldr: An agent learns to explore by modeling its own prediction errors, producing complex behaviors and more useful world representations.

paragraphs: This paper studies a scalable learning method that combines mini-batch stochastic gradients with random features. Random features provide a nonlinear sketch that approximates a kernel method, while stochastic updates reduce the work involved in processing training data. The question is how these computational choices affect statistical learning quality.

The estimator has no explicit penalty or constraint to regularize its solution. Instead, regularization arises implicitly through choices such as the number of random features, training iterations, step size, and mini-batch size. The authors analyze how these parameters control the learned solution, connecting implementation decisions with the model's ability to learn from finite data.

Under standard assumptions, they derive optimal finite-sample bounds and use numerical experiments to illustrate and corroborate the results. The significance is that approximation and optimization parameters have statistical roles as well as computational ones. Understanding them together provides a principled account of how an efficient approximate kernel learner can be controlled without an explicit regularization term.
neurips-2018-learning-with-sgd-and-rando.tldr: The paper derives optimal finite-sample bounds explaining implicit regularization in mini-batch stochastic-gradient learning with random features.

paragraphs: This paper asks how many observations are needed to learn a mixture of k Gaussian distributions in d dimensions. Accuracy is measured in total variation distance, which compares distributions. The authors establish matching necessary and sufficient sample scaling of Θ(kd²/ε²) for error ε, improving both previously known upper and lower bounds.

For mixtures of axis-aligned Gaussians, they show that O(kd/ε²) samples suffice, matching a known lower bound. The different dependence on dimension distinguishes this more structured family from general Gaussian mixtures. These are sample-complexity results: they quantify the amount of data required to achieve the stated distributional accuracy.

The upper bounds come from a new distribution-learning technique based on sample compression. A distribution class with a suitable compression scheme can be learned from few samples, and the property carries over to products and mixtures. Showing that multivariate Gaussians admit efficient sample compression supplies the key ingredient. This also makes the proof technique useful beyond the single mixture-learning result.
neurips-2018-nearly-tight-sample-complex.tldr: Sample compression yields nearly tight data requirements for learning Gaussian mixtures and a reusable framework for distribution learning.

paragraphs: A learned dynamics model predicts how an environment changes after an action. Models focused on pixel-level motion can struggle when familiar objects appear in unfamiliar arrangements. This paper introduces the Object-Oriented Dynamics Predictor, or OODP, which represents an environment through objects and predicts their behavior using actions and relationships among those objects.

OODP is an end-to-end neural network that can be trained without supervision. Its convolutional relation mechanism is specific to object classes rather than individual objects and uses a locality principle. This design supports transferring learned relationships across arrangements, instead of tying every interaction pattern to the particular objects encountered during training.

Experiments show substantially better generalization than previous methods across environments with different object layouts. The model learns from very few environments and accurately predicts dynamics in many unseen ones. Its learned dynamics are also semantically and visually interpretable. Together, these findings support object-based relational structure as a useful way to organize predictions for transfer to new layouts.
neurips-2018-object-oriented-dynamics-pr.tldr: OODP predicts action-dependent object dynamics through class-based local relations, improving generalization to unfamiliar object layouts.

paragraphs: Many datasets require overlapping groups: a person can belong to several communities, and a word can relate to several topics. This paper studies models that represent each item as a nonnegative weighted combination of exemplars belonging to only one group, with a small amount of noise. Those weights describe the item's mixed membership.

The shared structure has a geometric interpretation: the data form a cone whose corners correspond to the exemplars. This formulation encompasses mixed-membership network models, their degree-corrected variants, and topic models such as LDA. The authors use that common geometry to develop one inference approach that applies across these different model families.

Their algorithm, SVM-cone, uses a simple one-class support vector machine and provides provably consistent parameter inference for models of the stated form. Experiments on simulated and real datasets support both accuracy and scalability. The contribution is a unifying computational route: recovering overlapping memberships through shared geometric structure rather than designing an unrelated inference procedure for every application.
neurips-2018-overlapping-clustering-mode.tldr: SVM-cone uses shared cone geometry to provide scalable, provably consistent inference for several overlapping-cluster model families.

paragraphs: Sequential Attend, Infer, Repeat, or SQAIR, is a generative model that represents image sequences in terms of objects. Its latent variables explicitly encode how many objects are present, where they are, and what they look like. This organization makes the representation interpretable and supports discovering and tracking objects across successive frames.

The model can also generate future frames conditionally, simulating expected object motion. It extends Attend, Infer, Repeat while retaining unsupervised learning through structural inductive biases. Temporal consistency is central: information about an object across frames helps the model handle situations where the evidence in a single image is incomplete or ambiguous.

On moving multi-MNIST sequences, the authors show that SQAIR overcomes difficulties its predecessor has with overlapping or partly hidden objects. They also apply it to pedestrian CCTV footage, where it learns to detect, track, and generate walking pedestrians without supervision. The results connect explicit object representations with the practical benefits of using continuity over time.
neurips-2018-sequential-attend-infer-rep.tldr: SQAIR learns interpretable object representations from video without supervision, using temporal consistency to detect, track, and generate moving objects.

paragraphs: Unsupervised learning involves choices about what structure should count as useful, even when the target dataset has no labels. This paper proposes learning how to make those choices from a repository of supervised datasets. The source datasets can come from heterogeneous domains, while the resulting knowledge transfers to new unsupervised problems.

The framework reduces these decisions to supervised learning and provides a principled way to evaluate unsupervised algorithms. For clustering, it can help select an algorithm and the number of groups, as well as remove outliers. The authors establish agnostic bounds for several unsupervised problems and show how the framework provably circumvents Kleinberg's impossibility result.

Experiments across hundreds of problems show performance improvements using simple algorithms despite the diversity of the source domains. The framework also supports learning shared features with deep networks across many small datasets and performing zero-shot learning. Its central contribution is to make experience from previously supervised problems inform how structure is sought in new unlabeled data.
neurips-2018-supervising-unsupervised-le.tldr: A framework transfers experience from supervised datasets to guide and evaluate learning on new unsupervised datasets.

paragraphs: A classifier's prediction and its confidence in that prediction are separate from whether the prediction deserves trust. This paper proposes an additional signal, the trust score, which measures agreement between the classifier and a modified nearest-neighbor classifier on a test example. It assesses a prediction through comparison with another data-based decision.

Empirically, high scores identify correct predictions with high precision, while low scores identify incorrect ones with high precision. In the reported evaluations, this approach consistently outperforms the classifier's confidence score and many other baselines. The result concerns identifying which predictions are likely right or wrong, rather than simply improving the classifier's overall accuracy.

The paper also supplies a theoretical connection under mild distributional assumptions: high or low trust scores imply likely agreement or disagreement with the Bayes-optimal classifier. Its guarantees include finite-sample rates of statistical consistency in several nonparametric settings. These conditional results help explain the empirical behavior while preserving the distinction between a useful trust signal and certainty about any individual prediction.
neurips-2018-to-trust-or-not-to-trust-a-.tldr: A nearest-neighbor-based trust score identifies likely classifier errors more effectively than confidence scores in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Recognizing an action in a video does not by itself identify the pixels where that action occurs. VideoCapsuleNet addresses classification and pixel-wise action segmentation together in a unified network. It extends capsule networks from images to sequences of video frames, representing action information through a three-dimensional capsule architecture.

That extension greatly increases the number of capsules and makes routing expensive. The authors introduce capsule pooling to make the voting procedure tractable. Class-specific capsules support action localization, and parameterized skip connections from convolutional capsule layers further improve it. The whole network is trained end to end using both classification and localization losses.

The paper reports state-of-the-art results on UCF-Sports, J-HMDB, and the 24-class UCF-101 action-detection dataset. Reported v-mAP improvements are approximately 20% on UCF-101 and 15% on J-HMDB. These findings support a unified capsule-based approach that combines recognition with localization, while the pooling mechanism addresses the computational cost of bringing capsule routing into video.
neurips-2018-videocapsulenet-a-simplifie.tldr: VideoCapsuleNet jointly classifies and localizes actions using a 3D capsule network with pooling that makes video routing tractable.

paragraphs: Inferring a person's goal from their actions often assumes they act nearly optimally. When behavior looks inefficient, existing models may attribute it to randomness or a known bias. This paper considers another explanation: the person may misunderstand how actions affect the environment, so their decisions reflect an incorrect internal model of its dynamics.

The key idea is that behavior can be poor under the real rules yet sensible under the rules the person believes. The proposed method estimates those internal beliefs from observed actions and uses them to infer intent. This separates what someone wants from their understanding of how to achieve it, giving apparently suboptimal actions an informative interpretation.

Simulation experiments and a study with 12 participants show more accurate modeling of human intent. The approach also supports applications in shared-autonomy assistance and preference inference. These findings suggest that accounting for mistaken beliefs can improve how another agent interprets and assists a user, especially when observed actions are near-optimal under the user's internal model.
neurips-2018-where-do-you-think-you-re-g.tldr: Inferring a person's mistaken beliefs about environmental dynamics can improve intent prediction and support more useful assistance.
